question: A 3-day-old baby with ambiguous genitalia has the following results: karyotype 46,XX; markedly elevated serum 17-OHP; sodium 128 mEq/L; potassium 6.8 mEq/L; pelvic USG shows a uterus. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mixed gonadal dysgenesis typically shows a 45,X/46,XY karyotype and does not produce salt-wasting or elevated 17-OHP. This karyotype is 46,XX.

Correct. 46,XX + markedly elevated 17-OHP (the substrate that accumulates when 21-hydroxylase is blocked) + hyponatraemia/hyperkalaemia (salt-wasting) + uterus present = classic CAH due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. This is the COMMONEST cause of ambiguous genitalia in India.
CAIS presents as 46,XY with female external genitalia, absent uterus and absent Mullerian structures. This baby has 46,XX karyotype and a uterus — CAIS does not fit.

Ovotesticular DSD (true hermaphroditism) is rare and typically has a 46,XX or 46,XX/46,XY karyotype but does not characteristically present with the biochemical triad of elevated 17-OHP and salt-wasting.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key discriminator is the 17-OHP result. Markedly elevated 17-OHP in a 46,XX infant with salt-wasting and a uterus = CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency) — the commonest DSD cause in India.

Well done. The diagnostic triad for 21-hydroxylase deficiency (classic salt-wasting CAH): 46,XX karyotype + markedly elevated 17-OHP + electrolyte pattern of salt-wasting (low Na, high K). Urgent glucocorticoid + mineralocorticoid replacement is life-saving.
